headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:42: Fluke Steady, Bass Gone Nocturnal, Bonito Scouts Off the Block
subhead: The Ledge tide windows are still paying off in daylight — but the real bite has moved to the dark, and the bonito are starting to show their cards.
body_markdown:
Six-forty-two this morning, SW Ledge went dead slack. I had the boat parked over twenty-eight to thirty-four feet with marks stacked tight to the bottom before the current even hinted at swinging the other way. That five, six-minute window right at the turn is when you get one clean drift before the rip starts working again, and this week that's exactly when the fluke wanted to eat.

Let me be straight about what's happening out there right now, because I don't like selling a slow week as a hot one. The fluke bite off the Ledge and down toward the Harbor of Refuge rocks is steady, not explosive. We're picking through a mix of shorts and keepers on almost every drift — four, five keepers to a trip in that 19 to 22-inch range, with the occasional four-pounder mixed in. Nothing blitz-level, but it's dependable, and dependable is worth something in August. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails have been the ticket in that 28-34 foot band, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. Once the tide builds past mid-stage, I've had better luck dropping to a 1-ounce head just to hold bottom and keep contact with the structure. We flagged a couple weeks back that this fluke pattern would stay steady rather than turn into a blitz, and that's exactly how it's playing out — keeper-size fish mixed with shorts on almost every structure drift, nothing dramatic, just consistent work if you put in the drifts.

Striped bass have gone quiet in the daylight, and there's a reason for it. Surface temps have been sitting in that low-to-mid 70s range across the Sound and out toward the Block, which is right at the edge of what stripers tolerate comfortably during the day. They're not gone — they've just gone down and gone nocturnal. My best bass action this week has come after dark, working the SW Ledge rip on the last two hours of the outgoing with eels and bunker chunks fished tight to bottom in that same 25-35 foot zone. We've also had success drifting off North Light after 9 PM on the incoming, working big soft plastics slow along the bottom where the current pinches around the rocks. Nothing giant — mostly 24 to 30-inch fish with the occasional better one mixed in — but they're eating with confidence once the sun's down and the water cools a couple degrees. If you're set up to fish nights, this is the pattern right now. Daytime bass fishing at the Ledge has been mostly dead unless you're right on the turn of the tide when the cooler water briefly gets pushed up from below.

Now the part everybody's been asking about at the dock — bonito. We're seeing scout fish. Not a push yet, but scouts, which is exactly what you'd expect three weeks out from the new moon. I had two flash through a spread of Point Jude glass minnows off Sandy Point on Sunday, and a charter working the rip off Clay Head reported the same thing — quick, aggressive, gone in seconds. That's the tell. We called this pattern building last week, saying to expect more scout reports as the seasonal bait and temperature triggers lined up, and here they are right on schedule. The building tides toward the August 12th new moon are the trigger everybody in this corridor is watching. Once that tidal push strengthens, Block Island Sound is usually one of the first mainland-adjacent zones to see albies and bonito commit for real, and the squid and bait building around the island right now suggest we're close.

Bluefish have been the reliable bonus fish all week, and a good one — 3 to 6-pound blues mixed right into the fluke drifts off the Ledge, plus a stronger showing of bigger fish, 8 to 10 pounds, working the surface off Sandy Point in the early morning on peanut bunker imitations and small metal. If you want non-stop action for a few hours, that's your play — small Deadly Dicks or 1-ounce Kastmasters worked fast on the surface.

Black sea bass remain the honest bycatch on any bottom drift around the Ledge structure or the reef pockets off the southeast corner of the island — 14 to 17 inches mostly, biting squid strips and small jigs fished right on the bottom.

Looking ahead: if the tidal build continues clean into the new moon window, I expect the bonito scouts to turn into a real showing sometime in the next week to ten days, most likely first around Sandy Point and Clay Head where the rips concentrate bait hardest. The bass pattern should stay nocturnal until we get either a real cooling trend or that new moon current stirs the water column enough to push cooler bottom water up during the day. If a front comes through and knocks temps down even a couple degrees, watch for stripers to shift back to a more traditional daytime rip bite at the Ledge — that's the wildcard worth watching this week.
